title: Claude Certified Architect Professional – Full Course
note: Not included yet: 4 episodes (Ep15 Lifecycle & Docs, Ep16 Developer Productivity, and two practice-question videos). This page covers the first 16 videos.

episodes.title: Dec 7 updates
episodes.summary: The Claude exams get revised guides on 7 December. Developer foundations and architect professional move to version 1.1, while architect foundations is not on the update list. The ideas stay the same; the questions become scenario-based and the domain weights move.
keyPoints: Revised guides came out on 17 November; the revised exams go live on 7 December, and an exam booked before that date is still the old version.
Developer foundations, architect professional and associate foundations are named in the update; architect foundations is not changed.
Both revised exams keep 70 items (60 scored, 10 unscored trial items), 120 minutes, a 720 pass mark and the same prices.
Both are officially scenario-based multiple choice, which formalises what architect professional already was.

On architect professional, stakeholder communication and lifecycle management halves from 14% to 7%, while technical depth, governance, safety and risk rises from 14% to 16% and integration from 19% to 21%.
The exam date decides the blueprint: before 7 December use the old guide, on or after it use the new one.
A new developer professional certification is soft-launched through the partner academy, which needs a company or consultancy email.
traps: Restarting your prep because of the update; the concepts did not change, only the weighting and the wrapper.
Changing your prep for architect foundations, which is untouched.
Skipping an item because it may be an unmarked trial item; trial items cannot be spotted and carry no marks, so answer everything.
Same 120 minutes with more items: flag-and-move discipline matters more.

episodes.title: Course launch
episodes.summary: The launch video for the free professional course. It compares the foundations and professional exams, stresses the three professional-only domains, and explains the exam logistics such as format, retakes and renewal.
keyPoints: The professional exam tests whether you can own a Claude system end to end, including the stakeholder conversations, not only design it.

The three professional-only domains are governance, safety and risk (14%), stakeholder communication and lifecycle management (14%), and developer productivity and operational enablement (7%), together 35%.
Integration is the heaviest domain at 19%.
The format is 63 questions in 120 minutes, with single-answer and multiple-response items.
Retakes wait 14 days, then 30, then 90, with at most four attempts in a rolling 12 months; renewal done on time is free and non-proctored.
The exam is delivered through Pearson VUE, online-proctored or at a test centre, with 12-month validity.
traps: Multiple-response items are all or nothing, so one wrong choice scores zero.
Professional items are standalone with no surrounding context, so they can feel harder than the foundations exam.
A foundations pass does not cover the professional-only domains.
Guessing is not penalised, so never leave an answer blank.

episodes.title: Ep01 Solution Design & Architecture
episodes.summary: Starts domain 1 by turning a business problem into a Claude-based design, working from the problem towards the model. It introduces the four-part architecture, the "can versus should" test and the five value pillars as the tiebreaker between valid options.
keyPoints: Professional questions ask which architecture fits a stated business constraint, not what a term means.
Every cloud solution has four parts: input ingestion, processing, output and a feedback loop.
The processing layer can use a fast cheap model for classification and a stronger one for resolution, with tools called in between.
Prefer a deterministic lookup, rules engine or simple classifier when the answer is fixed, latency is hard or accuracy must be perfect.
The five value pillars are efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs; the pillar the stakeholder prioritises breaks ties.
The feedback loop has outcome tracking, quality metrics, operational metrics, user signals and drift detection, each tied to a pillar.
Scan each stem for the input, the constraint and the feedback loop; this usually removes two options.
traps: Choosing the most impressive-sounding option instead of the one that meets the stated constraint.
Adding an LLM to a task a rule or lookup could solve, which adds cost, latency and failure modes.
A design with no feedback loop is only a demo; logging that is not tied to a business pillar is not a feedback loop.
A sub-200 ms requirement rules out multi-step agentic designs.

episodes.title: Ep02 Architecture Patterns
episodes.summary: How to pick between workflow, agentic and augmented-LLM patterns by matching each to a constraint, and when hub-and-spoke multi-agent is the wrong answer. It also separates prompt chaining from dynamic decomposition and names capability bloat as a tested anti-pattern.
keyPoints: Workflow means the steps are fixed at design time; agentic means the model chooses the next step in a loop; augmented LLM is a single call with retrieval or a tool.
An agentic loop is perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat: good for open-ended work, but costlier, slower and harder to audit.
Latency and predictability favour workflow, a cost ceiling favours augmented LLM, and unknown steps favour agentic.
In hub-and-spoke, a coordinator routes all traffic, decomposes, delegates, aggregates and handles failures; sub-agents never talk to each other.
Skip multi-agent when one well-prompted agent can do it, when the latency budget is tight, or when you can already decompose the task.
Use prompt chaining when you know the steps in advance and dynamic decomposition when findings decide the next step.
Capability bloat: every tool adds prompt tokens and lowers tool-selection accuracy, so give each agent only what it needs.
Start with augmented LLM, move to workflow when one call is not enough, and go agentic only when steps cannot be predicted.
traps: Picking agentic because it is the buzzword.
Treating multi-agent as the default.
Adding tools or sub-agents "in case".
Using one augmented call when the work has fixed separate stages.
Calling a single call with a tool an agentic loop; one tool call is not a loop.

episodes.title: Ep03 Decomposition & Business Value
episodes.summary: Closes domain 1 with three ways to split a problem, the over-decomposition anti-pattern and the value pillars as the tiebreaker. It then explains why LLM systems offer statistical rather than per-response SLAs and three patterns for meeting them.
keyPoints: Decomposition comes in functional (by capability), data (by input type) and temporal (by phase) forms, and real systems mix them.
Over-decomposition adds overhead, latency, error surface and token cost; the right answer is often fewer components.
Split only when a subtask truly needs something different, such as another model tier, tools or context.
Efficiency is per unit of work, cost is total spend; transformation, productivity and performance SLAs are the other pillars.
The pillars conflict, so every architecture is a configuration of trade-offs.
When two designs are valid, the stakeholder named in the stem decides which pillar wins.
LLM systems give statistical guarantees over a population of requests, while deterministic code can promise per-request correctness.
Meet SLAs with confidence-based routing, statistical monitoring over a rolling window and graceful degradation with a fallback.
traps: Over-decomposing to look elegant.
Mixing up efficiency (per unit) with cost (total spend).
Parallelising steps that depend on each other, even if it cuts latency.
Promising per-response accuracy for an LLM component.

episodes.title: Ep04 Model Selection & System Prompts
episodes.summary: Treats model choice as an architectural decision based on task complexity, latency and cost, including tiered multi-model designs. It also covers thinking modes, settings that newer models reject, and how to write production system prompts and place guardrails.
keyPoints: There is no "best model" without a constraint set; start with Sonnet and move up only if the task proves too hard.
Opus gives the highest reasoning at the highest cost and latency, Sonnet is the balanced workhorse, Haiku is fastest and cheapest for classification and routing.
The three-axis matrix is task complexity, then latency budget, then cost ceiling as the tiebreaker.
A tiered design uses Haiku as intake, Sonnet for most generation and Opus for the hard minority.
On newer models, non-default temperature, top P or top K, and a fixed thinking budget, return a 400 error, so old code breaks on migration.
Replace vague judgment words and self-reported confidence with explicit categorical rules and an exact output format.
Prompt-level guardrails are probabilistic; hard policies belong in code through pre- and post-tool hooks.
traps: Defaulting to Opus for every call.
Carrying temperature or top-K settings from an older model to a newer one.
Trusting the model's confidence score, which is not calibrated to your team's standards.
Trust collapse: too many false positives make developers ignore every finding.
Enforcing a hard policy with a prompt instruction instead of a hook.

episodes.title: Ep05 Prompt Engineering, Context Windows & Caching
episodes.summary: Closes domain 2: choosing prompt techniques for a constraint, placing information in the context window, and prompt caching. It also compares skills, which load on demand, with CLAUDE.md, which is always loaded.
keyPoints: Zero-shot suits tight latency or a tight token budget, few-shot suits an exact output format, chain-of-thought suits complex multi-step tasks at a latency cost.
Use two to four few-shot examples, each with an input, a reason and an output; label-only examples encourage pattern matching.
Put instructions first, then examples, then retrieved context, with the user's query at the bottom.
Facts in the middle of a long prompt get less attention, so put critical IDs and amounts at the start or the end.
The cached prefix runs tools, then system prompt, then messages; cache reads cost about 90% less and a 5-minute write about 25% more.
The usage object shows cache creation and cache read tokens, which is how you confirm caching works.
Cache killers are timestamps in the system prompt, reordered tools, a flipped thinking configuration and a TTL that expires between sparse calls.
A skill shows only its name and description until needed; CLAUDE.md is always loaded.
traps: Chain-of-thought under a tight latency budget.
Many few-shot examples on high-variety input.
Burying key facts in the middle of a long prompt.
Putting a timestamp in the system prompt, which invalidates the cache.
Expecting caching to help short prompts or low-traffic endpoints; it fails silently.
Putting always-needed guidance in a skill instead of CLAUDE.md, or the reverse.

episodes.title: Ep06 RAG, Chunking & Retrieval
episodes.summary: The RAG pipeline from ingestion to generation, with chunking styles, index types and retrieval strategies matched to the data. It adds re-ranking and the rule that answers going wrong after a data refresh point to the retrieval layer first.
keyPoints: RAG is an architecture choice; for a corpus under about 200,000 tokens you can often put everything in the prompt, especially with caching.
Offline you ingest, chunk, embed and index; per request you embed the query, retrieve and generate.
Fixed-size chunking suits uniform text, semantic chunking follows topic shifts, and structure-aware chunking suits legal and technical documents.
Contextual retrieval adds a short context sentence to each chunk before embedding so it keeps its meaning.
Pure vector search misses exact codes, so hybrid vector plus BM25 covers both meaning and identifiers.
Metadata filters handle time, tenant or access scope.
Re-ranking retrieves many candidates and passes only the best few to Claude.
After a refresh, check stale embeddings, lost chunk context, index drift and an outdated chunker before blaming the model.
traps: Blaming the prompt or the model when retrieval changed after a refresh.
Fixed-size chunks on structured documents.
Pure vector search for exact error codes.
Using RAG for a corpus that fits in the prompt.
Letting the model answer when retrieval found nothing; add an explicit "context does not contain this" rule.

episodes.title: Ep07 MCP, Auth & Capability Bloat
episodes.summary: How an agent connects to the outside world: which protocol, acting as whom, and with what powers. It covers MCP setup, token rules, least privilege in layers, and why too many tools hurt.
keyPoints: Each integration decision answers how (protocol), as whom (identity) and with what powers (capability).
MCP is a universal adapter: the client discovers the tools a server offers instead of hard-coding them.
A server can be offered through STDIO, HTTP, SSE or an in-process SDK.
Choose by constraint: several clients needing one auth and audit point suggests MCP, a mature CLI suggests using the CLI, another team's autonomous agent suggests agent-to-agent.
MCP tokens have an audience and must be checked by the server they were issued for; no token pass-through, and credentials stay out of the model's context.
Prompts are not permission controls; least privilege lives in configuration, credentials and server-side checks, with human approval for high-stakes actions.
Tool bloat lowers selection reliability, widens what an injected instruction can reach, costs tokens every request and adds audit work.
Tool choice "any" forces some tool call, "tool" forces one named tool, "auto" lets the model decide.
traps: Confused deputy: a tool running on an admin identity can do what the user could not.
"Never delete customer accounts" in a system prompt is a request, not a control.
Forwarding the client's token downstream is forbidden.
Progressive discovery is not security; deferred tools are still reachable.
Wrapping a mature CLI in a new MCP server.
Adding a tool "just in case".

episodes.title: Ep08 Observability & Latency
episodes.summary: How to see inside an LLM system and justify speed-versus-quality trade-offs. LLM failures are fluent, so a wrong answer still looks like a success, and only a quality layer catches it.
keyPoints: LLM failures are fluent: a wrong answer returns a normal success status, so infrastructure dashboards stay green.
A trace is one user request; each step is a span sharing a trace ID, and retrieval should be its own span.
Log trace ID, API request ID, token counts, cache hits, latency per step, tool results, retrieval doc IDs and index version, and stop reason.
Keep raw personal data out of general logs; capture full conversations only on a separate, sampled, time-limited path.
Monitoring has three layers: traces, metrics and quality; only the quality layer catches fluent failures.
Justify a trade-off with a latency budget and a number on each side: cost from traces and benefit from the eval set.
Take free latency first: static content first with caching, a smaller tier if evals hold, parallel lookups, then streaming.
Progressive discovery is lean but adds a round trip; monolithic loading is predictable but token-heavy, and large catalogs usually use a hybrid.
traps: When latency, errors and cost are flat but users complain, look at the quality layer, not the latency alert.
"Log every prompt and response indefinitely" detects nothing and creates a compliance problem.
Switching everything to the smallest model to hit a latency target quietly degrades accuracy.
Cutting retrieval depth to save time.
Putting the date or a user name in the system prompt breaks the cache.
Streaming does not help a downstream system that needs the full payload.
Breadth is not bloat: six used tools out of nine is fine.

episodes.title: Ep09 Evaluation Metrics
episodes.summary: Opens domain 4: teams need measured evidence, not a feeling that a change works. It covers the five metric families, golden data sets, stratified sampling, grading methods and the noise floor.
keyPoints: Latency and cost can be read from traces; accuracy, safety and security only show up in tests.
An aggregate score can hide a failing slice, such as 97% overall with handwritten receipts near 60%.
Stratified sampling splits traffic into buckets, samples each one, and measures accuracy per category.
A golden data set is hand-labelled, fixed over time, and includes edge cases and guard rows whose correct answer is null or a refusal.
Rule-based grading is cheap and reproducible, model grading scales but needs calibration, and humans are the gold standard on a sample.
A good judge uses explicit criteria, binary verdicts with a short reason, and is checked against human labels.
Before trusting a score change, re-run the unchanged system to measure the noise floor.
An evaluation framework is a gate: ship only if overall accuracy holds and no stratum drops more than two points.
traps: Adding more examples picked the same way gives a bigger, more confident, still wrong number.
Changing the headline metric on unrepresentative data.
Swapping the grader instead of fixing the questions.
Random sampling that hides the failing slice.
A bad judge is worse than none, because it turns errors into scores.

episodes.title: Ep10 A/B Testing & Failure Diagnosis
episodes.summary: How to prove a change helped and how to work out what broke. LLM A/B tests need grading, repeated samples and a fixed metric, and failures sort into integration, prompt, hallucination and model mismatch.
keyPoints: LLM quality can drift with no deploy on your side because the provider updates the model underneath you.
Web-style A/B testing struggles with non-determinism, graded quality and small effect sizes.
Change one variable per test and keep everything else pinned.
Both variants use the same frozen eval set, or a random split of live traffic in the same window, with the metric and threshold fixed first.
Run offline first to kill bad ideas cheaply, then online; do not stop at the first green day.
The four failure categories are integration, prompt, hallucination and model mismatch.
Switch the model last, because moving up a tier is a large cost jump.
Diagnose by stating the symptom with a number, gathering the cheapest evidence, and flipping the suspect that turns the failure on and off.
Roll out in steps such as 5%, 25%, 100%, watching quality at each step.
traps: Asking the model which prompt it prefers.
A one-day 5% canary with no threshold set in advance.
Picking the metric or threshold after seeing results.
A festival week or other concurrent event is a confounder.
Changing the model first because it is the loudest suspect.
For hallucination, raising effort or model tier instead of grounding and validation.
Upgrading the whole pipeline when only the hardest 10% fails.

episodes.title: Ep11 Cost Optimization
episodes.summary: Closes domain 4 with cost optimisation and monitoring. Cost per request must be tracked from the usage block, and the four levers are caching, model tiering, context discipline and batch.
keyPoints: Every response's usage block carries input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens; log it on every request.
Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens.
Spend is requests times tokens per request times price per token, and each factor has a lever.
Cache reads are a small fraction of base input price; a prefix cached but never reused is a loss.
Route by task complexity, and downgrade a slice only after the golden set shows it holds.
The Message Batches API gives about 50% off for work nobody waits on, processed within 24 hours, single-turn, no streaming, matched by custom_id.
Ask first whether anyone is waiting; then whether multi-turn tool calls are needed; if neither, use batch.
Alert on ratios and unit economics such as cost per request, not on raw spend.
Input drift and behaviour drift are caught by a scheduled golden-set run and by logging model and prompt versions.
traps: Tracking the monthly total instead of cost per request.
Choosing batch for the discount when a user or pipeline is waiting.
A blanket downgrade to the smallest tier.
Cutting retrieval depth without an accuracy check.
Buying a one-hour cache TTL for ordinary chat traffic.
Paging on raw spend when volume rises seasonally.
Putting dynamic fields such as the date in the cached prefix.

episodes.title: Ep12 Hooks, Guardrails & Risk
episodes.summary: Opens the governance part: a system prompt is steering, not a permission system, so guardrails must be enforced in code. It covers four layers of defence, hooks, the risk register, graceful degradation and escalation triggers.
keyPoints: A prompt is probabilistic and steers the model; it does not hold, so guardrails are a system-design concern.
Four layers: input validation, model constraints, output validation and tool gating.
Output is treated as untrusted: schema checks, leakage scans and grounding checks.
A PreToolUse hook can allow, deny or rewrite a call before it runs; a PostToolUse hook can rewrite the result.
A hook matcher compares only the tool name; the command or arguments are checked inside the hook code.
Flagging injected text only informs the model; least privilege decides what is possible.
Tool gating is the strongest layer: a prerequisite gate opens the refund tool for a fact the code established, not for a message saying "verified".
A fallback chain goes primary model, evaluated alternate tier, labelled last-known-good, queued work, then an honest error with a human path.
Escalate on an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or inability to progress.
traps: "Add a rule to the system prompt" is the distractor in about half of guardrail questions.
A matcher written as a command such as "rm -rf" never fires.
Detection is not defence.
Logging full untrusted ticket text is a leakage risk, not a control.
Retrying a failing primary endpoint hammers it and hides the outage.
Silently routing everything to a smaller tier when only simple claims were evaluated.
Negative sentiment alone is not an escalation trigger.

episodes.title: Ep13 Compliance, Ethics & HITL
episodes.summary: Finishes domain 5 with human review, compliance rulebooks and ethics. A system can run flawlessly and still not be allowed to run as it does, so someone must be able to answer for each action.
keyPoints: Human in the loop means a person with real authority reviews the output before the outcome stands; someone who only watches is in the audience.
Review is mandatory for high stakes, irreversible outcomes, regulated review and low confidence.
A confidence score is a safety signal only after calibration against labelled data, and thresholds are business dials.
A review queue has arithmetic, so justify it with numbers; "review everything" is a cost answer, not a design.
Which rulebook applies depends on whose data is touched: HIPAA for US health data, FedRAMP for US federal cloud data, GDPR for EU residents' personal data.
Compliance is a property of the data flow: minimise at intake, log with identity, and keep a deletion path to every store.
When a rulebook demands isolation, segment the environment instead of routing by rule.
Bias is detected by stratified evaluation and counterfactual tests where only the identity signal is swapped.
Transparency means logging the decision, the inputs that drove it, the confidence and any sign-off.
traps: A random 5% sample does not satisfy a rule requiring review of every denial.
Negative sentiment is not an escalation trigger.
Routing all volume to humans is a second call centre, not a design.
Trusting an aggregate pass rate.
Stripping names alone leaves proxies such as addresses.
An "AI-assisted" disclosure is not mitigation.
A shared pipeline with a disclaimer fails once two rulebooks apply.

episodes.title: Ep14 Stakeholder Communication
episodes.summary: Opens domain 6: gathering requirements, explaining recommendations and setting promises a real system can keep. The human constraint often decides the architecture as much as the technical one.
keyPoints: Structured discovery runs in order: business objective, success metrics, data landscape, then constraints; solutions come last.
Ask downside questions in every meeting: what happens when this is wrong, who bears the cost, and what is the escalation path.
Translate technical facts into consequences: P95 is the worst 5% of moments, and cost per request is the meter.
Every recommendation travels with its rejected twin and the constraint that killed it.
An architecture decision record has four parts: the decision, the context, the alternatives rejected, and the reasoning.
An LLM system promises statistical guarantees over a population, with a measurement and a repair path.
Promise latency at the tail (P95 or P99) and cost as a range.
Say limitations early with numbers: the rate per stratum, how you will detect it, and the repair.
traps: Answering a solution question such as which model to buy before discovery.
A proof of concept that demonstrates the wrong thing if the objective changes.
Drafting an SLA before discovery.
Any option guaranteeing per-response correctness.
A "performance may vary" disclaimer does not rescue an impossible promise.
An optimisation sprint to hide a gap, or declaring the target impossible in writing.

questions.q: Your developer foundations exam is booked for 5 December and you prepared with guide version 1.0. The revised exams start on 7 December. What is the right move?
options: Cancel and rebook after 7 December so that you study the new weightings first, since the old exam will be retired immediately
Spend the remaining days relearning every concept, because the update rewrote the ideas behind the exam
Keep your 1.0 preparation and sit the exam, because the changes only apply from 7 December
Switch to the architect foundations track, because that is the exam the update changes the most
questions.explain: The exam date decides the blueprint: before 7 December the old guide applies. The concepts did not change, only weightings and format.

learnMore.en: Your exam date decides which guide you need. A 5 December exam is before the change, so your old preparation is still the right one. The ideas stayed the same anyway.
learnMore.hi: Exam ki date decide karti hai ki kaunsa guide lagega. 5 December, 7 December se pehle hai, to purani preparation hi sahi hai. Concepts waise bhi same hain.

questions.q: During a revised exam you meet an item that feels oddly unrelated to the rest. You suspect it is one of the ten unscored trial items. What should you do?
options: Answer it properly like any other item, since trial items look the same as scored ones
Skip it quickly to save time for the scored items, since unscored items carry no marks at all and cost you time
Give it a long careful answer since trial items are weighted more heavily than the rest
Flag it and leave it blank so the exam board can see you recognised it as a trial item
questions.explain: Unmarked trial items cannot be spotted, so every item deserves a real answer.

learnMore.en: You cannot tell which items are the trial ones. If you skip a normal item by mistake, you lose marks. So answer everything.
learnMore.hi: Trial items pehchaan nahi sakte. Agar normal item skip kar diya to marks jaate hain. Isliye har item ka answer do.

questions.q: A legal startup must cut contract review from six hours to one hour. Option A is one augmented-LLM call with a checklist, and an associate reviews the flags. Option B is a multi-step agent with a precedent database and a research tool, more thorough but slower and dearer. Which fits, and why?
options: Option B, because more thorough research makes the better design for legal work
Option B, because multi-step agents are cheaper to run than a single augmented call
Neither, since contract review should not use a model without a rules engine in front of it
Option A, because the goal is efficiency and a single call with human review meets it
questions.explain: The stem is about efficiency, so the lighter design wins; B would suit a transformation goal.

learnMore.en: The stem says "save time", which is the efficiency pillar. One simple call plus a human check does that. The bigger agent is for a different goal.
learnMore.hi: Stem time bachane ki baat karta hai, yaani efficiency pillar. Ek simple call aur human check kaafi hai. Bada agent doosre goal ke liye hota hai.

questions.q: A healthcare firm summarises 50,000 claims a day in a standard format. The SLA is 3 seconds and accuracy must be above 95%. Which design fits?
options: A multi-step agent that plans, calls tools and checks its own work before writing each summary
A workflow of deterministic extraction and templates, with Claude only on the narrative parts
One augmented call with extended thinking switched on, so a single request does all the work
A parallel multi-agent setup with one sub-agent per section and a coordinator that merges the results
questions.explain: The agent and the extended-thinking call break the 3-second SLA, and parallel agents are unnecessary for a fixed format.

learnMore.en: Most of the job is fixed, so do it with plain code and templates. Use Claude only where writing is needed. This keeps it fast and cheap.
learnMore.hi: Zyada kaam fixed hai, to code aur template se karo. Claude sirf narrative hisse mein use karo. Isse speed aur cost dono theek rehte hain.

questions.q: A financial firm needs sub-200 ms responses with a full audit trail. A teammate proposes an agentic design with autonomous tool use. What is the best response?
options: Accept it, because autonomous tool use gives the most capable and flexible solution for finance
Reject it, because multi-step agent loops cannot meet the latency and audit constraints
Accept it but add a larger model so the loop finishes inside the 200 ms limit
Accept it and rely on streaming to make the responses feel faster to the user
questions.explain: A sub-200 ms requirement rules out multi-step agentic designs, and loops are harder to audit.

learnMore.en: Each loop step takes time, so a 200 ms limit leaves no room. Loops are also harder to audit. Pick the design that fits the stated limits.
learnMore.hi: Agent loop ke har step mein time lagta hai, 200 ms mein jagah nahi bachti. Audit bhi mushkil hota hai. Jo design limits mein fit ho, wahi chuno.

questions.q: A team ships a Claude-based triage tool with request logs but nothing connecting its results to the business goal. Reviewers say the design is incomplete. Why?
options: It lacks a larger model tier, so the logs are not processed quickly enough
It has too many logs, and logging more than input and output hurts latency
It does not use deterministic rules at each step, which is the required fourth component of a design
It has no feedback loop tied to a business pillar, so nobody can tell if it delivers value
questions.explain: A design without a feedback loop is a demo, and logging not tied to a pillar is not a feedback loop.

learnMore.en: A feedback loop checks results against what the business wants, like whether tickets stayed closed. Logs alone just store data.
learnMore.hi: Feedback loop result ko business goal se jodta hai, jaise ticket band raha ya nahi. Sirf logs data jama karte hain, feedback nahi dete.

questions.q: A task always has the same fixed answer, latency is hard and accuracy must be perfect. Which approach does the course prefer?
options: A deterministic lookup or rules engine rather than a model
A frontier model with extended thinking to maximise answer quality on every request
An agentic loop that can verify the answer several times before replying
A fine-tuned model that has learned the answers from past examples of the task
questions.explain: When the answer is fixed or accuracy must be perfect, adding an LLM adds cost, latency and failure modes.

learnMore.en: If the answer never changes, a lookup gives it every time, fast and for free. A model can add errors and delay for no gain.
learnMore.hi: Agar answer hamesha same hai, lookup har baar sahi aur fast deta hai. Model se sirf delay aur galti ka chance badhta hai.

questions.q: An insurer processes 5,000 claims a day, each needing the same five steps (extract, validate, classify, route, summarise) in under five seconds, with an audit trail and cost pressure. Which design fits?
options: A coordinator with four sub-agents, because splitting the work across agents is faster and more thorough
One augmented call with policy records pulled by RAG, because one call is always the cheapest option
A deterministic five-step prompt chain, because the steps are fixed and each one is traceable
An agentic loop that decides the order of steps for each claim, to handle unusual claims
questions.explain: A adds coordination overhead and path variants; C cannot perform five fixed stages in a single call.

learnMore.en: The steps never change, so fix them in a chain. Each step can be checked and timed. Agents or one big call do not help here.
learnMore.hi: Steps fixed hain, to chain banao. Har step check aur time ho sakta hai. Agents ya ek bada call yahan kaam nahi aate.

questions.q: Before building an agentic workflow, you ask whether you know the steps in advance. You do not, because each finding decides what to look at next. Which approach fits?
options: Prompt chaining, because it is the simplest pattern and works for most tasks
A single augmented call, because retrieval removes the need to plan steps
Hub-and-spoke with every sub-agent talking to the others to share what they find along the way
Dynamic decomposition, where steps are found at runtime from what each result shows
questions.explain: Use prompt chaining only when the steps are known ahead of time; use dynamic decomposition when findings drive the next step.

learnMore.en: When you cannot predict the next step, a fixed chain breaks. Let the model decide the next step from what it just found.
learnMore.hi: Jab agla step pehle se pata nahi, fixed chain toot jaati hai. Pichle result dekhkar agla step runtime par decide hone do.

questions.q: In which situation is a multi-agent hub-and-spoke design the wrong answer?
options: The work has to be split across many independent subtasks that need different tools at large scale and volume
One well-prompted agent with good tool descriptions can do the job within a tight latency budget
A coordinator is needed to aggregate results and handle failures from several specialists
The task is open-ended and the steps cannot be predicted at design time
questions.explain: Multi-agent adds coordination overhead and serial calls; skip it when one agent suffices or latency is tight.

learnMore.en: More agents mean more hand-offs and more waiting. If one agent can do the work, extra agents only add delay and cost.
learnMore.hi: Zyada agents ka matlab zyada hand-off aur intezaar. Ek agent kaam kar sakta hai to extra agents sirf delay aur cost badhate hain.

questions.q: A team keeps adding extra tools to its agent "in case they are needed". What problem does this create?
options: Little to worry about, because unused tools are ignored at run time
Higher cache hit rates, because more tools give the agent more stable context
Capability bloat: each tool adds prompt tokens and lowers tool-selection accuracy
Slower training of the model, because each tool must be learned before it can be used
questions.explain: Every tool adds tokens to the prompt and makes the right choice harder; give each agent only the tools it needs.

learnMore.en: Each tool description takes space in every request and gives the model one more thing to confuse. Keep only the tools needed.
learnMore.hi: Har tool ka description har request mein jagah leta hai aur model ko confuse karta hai. Sirf zaroori tools rakho.

questions.q: An engineer calls one model call that uses a single tool an "agentic loop". Is that correct?
options: No, because one tool call is not a loop; it is an augmented LLM
Yes, because using a tool at all makes a design agentic by definition
Yes, if the model is Opus, since smaller tiers lack the ability to loop
No, because agentic designs include a retrieval step first
questions.explain: An augmented LLM is a single call with retrieval or tools; a loop means perceive, reason, act, observe and repeat.

learnMore.en: A loop keeps going until the model decides it is done. One call with one tool just runs once, so it is an augmented LLM.
learnMore.hi: Loop mein model baar baar soch kar kaam karta hai. Ek call aur ek tool sirf ek baar chalta hai, isliye wo augmented LLM hai.

questions.q: A legal contract review uses five sequential sub-agents and takes 45 seconds, but the SLA is 20 seconds. Which change best fixes it?
options: Merge the first three agents into one with a well-structured prompt to remove round trips
Upgrade all five sub-agents to Opus so that every step reasons faster and more accurately than before
Add prompt caching and run all five agents in parallel to cut the wait
Add a sixth agent that supervises the other five and skips steps when it can
questions.explain: Opus is slower, caching only helps repeated content, and the steps are sequential so they cannot run in parallel.

learnMore.en: Each agent hand-off costs a round trip. Merging steps removes those trips. A bigger model or caching does not fix the waiting.
learnMore.hi: Har agent hand-off ek round trip hai. Steps merge karne se trips kam hote hain. Bada model ya caching is waiting ko theek nahi karte.

questions.q: MedInsure has two valid designs: one cuts cost with the cheapest model on simple appeals, the other guarantees a seven-day turnaround with accuracy. How do you choose?
options: Choose the cheaper design, because cost is the pillar that settles the debate
Choose the faster design, because SLAs outrank the other value pillars
Use the pillar the stem names for the stakeholder asking, since both designs are valid
Combine both designs fully, because the exam expects you to maximise all five pillars at the same time
questions.explain: The pillars conflict, so the stakeholder and priority named in the stem decide the answer.

learnMore.en: You cannot win on every pillar. The question tells you who is asking and what they care about. That pillar breaks the tie.
learnMore.hi: Sab pillars par jeet nahi sakte. Question batata hai kaun puch raha hai aur use kya chahiye. Wahi pillar tie todta hai.

questions.q: A design splits one simple task into six cooperating components "to look elegant". What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong, because more components means a cleaner separation of responsibility between parts
Over-decomposition adds overhead, latency and token cost; fewer components is often right
It should be split further, since each component must use its own model tier
It breaks the temporal pattern, which requires exactly three components for a task that is split up
questions.explain: Decompose only when a subtask genuinely needs a different model tier, tools or context.

learnMore.en: Every extra part costs time, tokens and a new place to fail. Split only when a part truly needs something different.
learnMore.hi: Har extra part mein time, tokens aur fail hone ki nayi jagah judti hai. Tabhi todo jab part ko sach mein kuch alag chahiye.

questions.q: A manager says "this change improves efficiency, so total spend will fall". What is the mix-up?
options: Nothing is wrong, because efficiency and cost move together in an LLM system of any size
Efficiency means latency, which is a performance SLA and has no link to cost
Total spend belongs to the transformation pillar, which covers the cost questions
Efficiency is per unit of work; total spend is the separate cost pillar
questions.explain: Efficiency is time or cost per unit; cost is total spend or ownership. The exam tests that they differ.

learnMore.en: Efficiency asks "how much per item". Cost asks "how much in total". A cheaper item can still mean a bigger bill if volume grows.
learnMore.hi: Efficiency matlab har item par kitna. Cost matlab kul kitna. Item sasta ho par volume badhe to bill phir bhi bada ho sakta hai.

questions.q: A client asks you to guarantee that every response from the Claude component is correct. What is the best way to set the SLA?
options: Promise per-response correctness, because that is what a production SLA must mean
Promise 100% accuracy on average and add a disclaimer in the contract for exceptions that appear
State a statistical guarantee over many requests, backed by routing, monitoring and a fallback
Refuse to give an SLA, since model output is too hard to measure against a target
questions.explain: Only deterministic code can promise per-request correctness; LLM systems offer population-level guarantees.

learnMore.en: A model can be wrong on a single answer. What you can promise is a rate over many requests, and a plan for the misses.
learnMore.hi: Model ek single answer mein galat ho sakta hai. Tum bahut requests par ek rate promise kar sakte ho, aur misses ka plan.

questions.q: A help-desk SaaS handles 10,000 queries a day with a 3-second target and a $5,000 monthly AI budget. Everything runs on Opus and customers complain about speed. Which fix fits?
options: A tiered design: Haiku routes simple queries, Sonnet does standard support, Opus takes escalations
Turn on extended thinking on Opus so each answer is reached with fewer retries and less delay
Move all traffic to Haiku, because the fastest and cheapest tier solves both complaints at once for the team
Shorten the system prompt, since prompt length is the main cause of slow replies here
questions.explain: The core issue is Opus on every query; shrinking the prompt or thinking harder does not remove it.

learnMore.en: Most queries are easy, so they do not need the biggest model. Send easy ones to small models and keep Opus for the hard few.
learnMore.hi: Zyada queries aasaan hain, unhe bade model ki zaroorat nahi. Aasaan chhote model ko do, Opus sirf mushkil queries ke liye.

questions.q: A claims system handles 50,000 claims a day with a two-second classification step and a $0.02 average cost ceiling. Which tier split fits?
options: Opus for every claim, since top reasoning protects against costly assessment mistakes
Sonnet for classification and Haiku for assessment, because the cheaper tier suits the harder work better
Haiku for all steps, because the cost ceiling is the only constraint in the stem
Haiku classifies every claim, Sonnet assesses the bulk, Opus takes only the small complex share
questions.explain: All-Opus would overshoot the ceiling by four to five times; tiering keeps the blended cost under it.

learnMore.en: Use the cheap fast model where the task is simple, and the strong model only where needed. The average cost then stays under the limit.
learnMore.hi: Simple kaam par sasta fast model, mushkil kaam par strong model. Isse average cost limit ke neeche rehta hai.

questions.q: A team migrates code to a newer Claude model and keeps its old temperature and top-K settings. What happens?
options: The settings are silently ignored, so outputs become a little less varied than they were before
A 400 error is returned, so the old code breaks instead of degrading
The model accepts them but halves its thinking budget to compensate
The settings still work, if adaptive thinking is turned off
questions.explain: On newer models, non-default temperature, top P, top K and fixed thinking budgets return an error; steering moves to prompts and effort.

learnMore.en: Newer models do not accept those settings any more. The call fails with an error. Steer with prompts and the effort setting instead.
learnMore.hi: Naye models in settings ko accept nahi karte, call error deti hai. Ab prompt aur effort setting se steer karo.

questions.q: A policy says the agent must never issue refunds above a set amount. Where should this be enforced?
options: In the system prompt with strong wording, since the model follows written policy reliably
In code, with a pre-tool hook that blocks the refund, since prompt rules are only probabilistic
In the output format section, by asking the model to confirm the limit in each reply
In the model's own confidence score, by refusing whenever confidence drops under a chosen threshold level
questions.explain: Hard policies belong in code; nuanced guidance belongs in the prompt.

learnMore.en: A prompt asks the model nicely, and it may still slip. Code checks the refund every time. Use code for hard rules.
learnMore.hi: Prompt model se request karta hai, kabhi chook sakta hai. Code har baar refund check karta hai. Hard rule ke liye code use karo.

questions.q: A code-review prompt says "be thorough and conservative" and asks the model to report only findings above 80% confidence. Developers still ignore the output because of false positives. What is the better fix?
options: Raise the confidence threshold to 95%, since a stricter number removes the false positives
Add stronger adjectives such as "extremely careful" to push precision higher
Switch to Opus, because only the largest model can judge its own confidence correctly
Replace the judgment words with explicit categorical rules and an exact output format
questions.explain: Vague words and self-reported confidence do not improve precision, and the model's confidence is not calibrated to your standards.

learnMore.en: Words like "thorough" mean different things each time. Clear rules say exactly what to report and how. That cuts false alarms.
learnMore.hi: "Thorough" jaise words ka matlab har baar badal jata hai. Clear rules batate hain kya report karna hai aur kaise. Isse false alarms kam hote hain.

questions.q: A pipeline reads 500 claim documents a day, about 5,800 input tokens each (2,000 instructions, 800 tool definitions, 3,000 chunk). Input costs about $12,000 a month. Which change has the most leverage?
options: Cache the stable prefix of tools, system prompt and examples, leaving the chunk uncached
Move the instructions to the end of the prompt, after the chunk, so that the model reads them last
Add chain-of-thought to each call so the model needs fewer follow-up requests
Drop the tool definitions from the request and describe the tools in plain text each time
questions.explain: The tools and instructions are identical each call, so caching them cuts input cost by about 40%.

learnMore.en: Most of the prompt repeats on every call. Cache that part, so you pay much less for it. Only the new chunk is full price.
learnMore.hi: Prompt ka zyada hissa har call mein repeat hota hai. Use cache karo, to kam paise lagte hain. Sirf naya chunk full price hota hai.

questions.q: A support agent handles 200 requests an hour, with a 3,000-token system prompt and examples plus a 2,000-token history per customer. How do you reduce input cost?
options: Cache the customer history too, because it is the part that changes most between one request and the next
Remove the examples from the prompt, because the system prompt is too long for caching
Turn on prompt caching so the system prompt stays cached and only the history is fresh
Switch to a one-hour cache and put the customer name at the top of the system prompt
questions.explain: The system prompt is stable and shared, so it caches well; the per-customer history is unique per call.

learnMore.en: The shared system prompt is the same for everyone, so cache it. The customer history changes every time, so it stays fresh.
learnMore.hi: System prompt sabke liye same hai, use cache karo. Customer history har baar badalti hai, isliye wo fresh rehti hai.

questions.q: A team puts the current timestamp at the top of the system prompt, and cache reads suddenly drop to zero. Why?
options: Timestamps are blocked by the cache, so every request that contains one returns an error to the caller
The prompt now falls below the minimum cacheable size
The cache only works at night, when the timestamp in the prompt happens to stay the same as before
The changing timestamp alters the prefix, so every request misses the cache
questions.explain: A cache needs an identical prefix; a changing timestamp invalidates it, and no error is raised.

learnMore.en: The cache matches the start of the prompt exactly. If that start changes each time, nothing matches. Put changing things last.
learnMore.hi: Cache prompt ke shuru ko exact match karta hai. Shuru har baar badle to match nahi hota. Badalne wali cheezein aakhir mein rakho.

questions.q: A long prompt contains a policy ID and an amount that the answer depends on, buried halfway through the text. Answers are sometimes wrong. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: The model forgets IDs, so replace the policy ID with a long natural-language description
Facts in the middle get less attention, so move them to the start or the end
The context window is full, so the facts need to be repeated in the middle several times
The model prefers retrieved context, so remove the system prompt entirely
questions.explain: Information in the middle of a long prompt gets less attention ("lost in the middle").

learnMore.en: Models read the start and the end best. A key fact in the middle can be overlooked. Put important facts at the start or end.
learnMore.hi: Model start aur end sabse achhe se padhta hai. Beech ka fact chhoot sakta hai. Zaroori facts start ya end mein rakho.

questions.q: You add few-shot examples that only show an input and its label. The model copies the pattern and fails on new cases. What makes better examples?
options: Twenty or more examples that are bare labels, so the model sees each pattern
Examples that give just the output, since reasons make the prompt too long
Two to four examples, each with an input, a reason and an output
One example repeated, so the model gives the same answer each time
questions.explain: Label-only examples encourage pattern matching; the reason shows the rule, and many examples fill the window.

learnMore.en: If the example shows why, the model learns the rule, not just the pattern. A few good examples beat many bare ones.
learnMore.hi: Example mein "kyun" ho to model rule seekhta hai, sirf pattern nahi. Kuch achhe examples bahut saare simple examples se behtar hain.

questions.q: A guideline applies to every single interaction in a project, such as a coding convention. Where should it live?
options: In CLAUDE.md, because it is always loaded
In a skill, because skills are the right home for rules that must apply every time
In a few-shot example inside each user message
In a sub-agent that runs once a day and writes the rule back
questions.explain: CLAUDE.md is always loaded; a skill shows only its name and description until it is needed.

learnMore.en: CLAUDE.md is always read. A skill is loaded only when it is needed. A rule for every case belongs in the always-loaded file.
learnMore.hi: CLAUDE.md hamesha load hota hai. Skill zaroorat par load hota hai. Har case ka rule always-loaded file mein jaata hai.

questions.q: After a quarterly refresh of clinical protocols, the assistant returns outdated answers, while the prompt and model are unchanged. What should you investigate?
options: The retrieval and indexing pipeline, where stale embeddings may compete with new ones
Rewrite the system prompt to tell the model to prefer the newest protocol every time
Move to a larger model so that it can reason about which protocol version is the newer one
Lower the model temperature so older answers become less likely
questions.explain: Problems after a data refresh usually sit upstream of the model: stale embeddings, lost chunk context, index drift or an old chunker.

learnMore.en: The prompt and model did not change, but the data did. So check how the data was stored and found. Old entries may still be in the index.
learnMore.hi: Prompt aur model nahi badle, data badla. Isliye check karo data kaise store aur search ho raha hai. Purani entries index mein ho sakti hain.

questions.q: A support bot answers questions from natural-language troubleshooting guides and also from logs full of error codes. Users ask both kinds of question. Which retrieval fits?
options: Pure vector search, because embeddings capture exact error codes as well as meaning
BM25 alone, since keyword matching handles both kinds of question equally well
Hybrid retrieval: semantic search for how-to questions and BM25 for exact codes
Put the whole corpus in the prompt, because hybrid retrieval needs a re-ranker before it can work
questions.explain: Dense search matches meaning but can miss exact codes; BM25 handles identifiers; a mixed corpus needs both.

learnMore.en: Meaning-based search is good for how-to questions. Keyword search is good for exact codes. Using both covers both kinds.
learnMore.hi: Meaning wali search how-to ke liye achhi hai. Keyword search exact codes ke liye. Dono saath mein dono tarah ke sawal sambhalti hain.

questions.q: A legal Q&A system answers general termination questions but fails on specific clauses in named contracts. Its chunks are fixed 500-token blocks and the index is pure vector. Which fix is best?
options: Increase the chunk size to 2,000 tokens, keep the pure vector index, and add a longer system prompt for clause questions
Structure-aware chunking with contextual retrieval, a hybrid index and metadata filters
Switch to a larger model so that it can reason across the clauses that were split between two chunks
Add more examples of termination questions to the system prompt
questions.explain: Fixed chunks split nested clauses, pure vector search misses contract names, and there were no metadata filters.

learnMore.en: Legal documents have a clear structure, so cut them by clauses. Add the contract name to each piece and allow filters. Then specific clauses can be found.
learnMore.hi: Legal documents ka structure clear hota hai, isliye clause ke hisaab se kaato. Har piece mein contract ka naam aur filters jodo. Tab specific clause mil jata hai.

questions.q: In a RAG demo, a user asks for the company dress code, but the retrieved context has no such information. What is the right behaviour?
options: The model answers from general knowledge about what typical office dress codes tend to look like
The model retrieves more chunks until some text mentions clothing
The model politely refuses every question that was not covered in its last training data set
It says the context does not contain it, because the system prompt has an explicit rule
questions.explain: Without an explicit "the context does not contain this" rule, the model may guess when retrieval finds nothing.

learnMore.en: If the documents do not answer, the safe answer is "I do not know from these documents". Tell the model this in the system prompt.
learnMore.hi: Agar documents mein jawab nahi hai, to "in documents se pata nahi" kehna safe hai. Model ko system prompt mein yeh batao.

questions.q: A company has a 60,000-token handbook and plans a full RAG pipeline for it. What does the course suggest?
options: Build RAG anyway, since retrieval is cheaper than putting a long prompt in front of the model
Split the handbook into one-word chunks to make the retrieval step as exact as it can possibly be
Consider skipping RAG and putting the whole handbook in the prompt, with caching
Use RAG after first fine-tuning the model on the handbook text
questions.explain: Under about 200,000 tokens you can often skip RAG; it is an architecture choice, not a requirement.

learnMore.en: A small document fits in the prompt directly. A pipeline adds parts that can fail. With caching, the repeated cost is low too.
learnMore.hi: Chhota document seedha prompt mein aa jata hai. Pipeline mein fail hone wale parts badh jaate hain. Caching ke saath repeat cost bhi kam hota hai.

questions.q: A fintech compliance lookup is used from Claude Code, a chat app and two custom agents, owned by four teams. Security wants one place to enforce authorisation and audit every call. What should you do?
options: Expose the service as an MCP server so every client goes through one governed point
Let each team call the REST API directly, because direct calls are always the simplest
Wrap the service in an autonomous agent that the four teams message through agent-to-agent
Paste the API documentation into each client's system prompt so every team can query it
questions.explain: Several clients needing one auth and audit point is the case for MCP; prompts and A2A do not centralise enforcement.

learnMore.en: With four teams and different clients, you want one front door. An MCP server gives one place to check access and log every call.
learnMore.hi: Chaar teams aur alag clients hain, to ek hi darwaza chahiye. MCP server ek jagah access check aur har call ka log deta hai.

questions.q: A support agent has 14 tools. Two of them, issue refund and delete account, never fired in 90 days of logs. Security wants the risk reduced. What is the best fix?
options: Add a confirmation prompt before each of the two tools runs, so that a person must approve the call
Add detailed audit logging on every call to those two tools, so any misuse can be traced afterwards
Add a system prompt rule requiring manager approval before either tool is used
Remove both tools, since the other controls only wrap a capability that should not exist
questions.explain: Confirmation, logging and prompt rules are compensating controls wrapped around a capability that should not exist; an unused tool is pure risk.

learnMore.en: If nobody uses a tool, the safest choice is to take it away. Extra checks around a tool you do not need are just more work.
learnMore.hi: Jab koi tool use hi nahi hota, use hata dena sabse safe hai. Bekaar tool ke aas-paas extra checks sirf extra kaam hain.

questions.q: An IT agent has about 120 tools across six systems, all used weekly. Tool selection is slipping and definitions use a lot of context. It must stay a single agent with no extra coordination hop. What fits?
options: Cut the tools down, since every extra tool is a risk even when it is used every week by the team
Defer most tools behind tool search, keeping one agent with every tool reachable
Split into six sub-agents, one for each system, with a coordinator in front
Merge generic tools into a mode parameter so there are fewer definitions
questions.explain: Every tool is used, so cutting breaks work, and splitting adds a coordination hop that the stem rules out.

learnMore.en: All the tools are needed, so do not remove them. Load them only when needed through search. The agent stays single.
learnMore.hi: Sab tools kaam aate hain, isliye hatao mat. Search ke through zaroorat par load karo. Agent ek hi rehta hai.

questions.q: A system prompt says "never delete customer accounts", yet the agent holds an admin credential that can do it. Is the account safe?
options: Yes, because the model follows strongly worded rules in the system prompt every time it is asked to
No, since a prompt is only a request; enforce it in config, credentials or the server
Yes, as long as the prompt rule is repeated in the user message too
No, because the rule should be written in a longer format with several worked examples in the prompt
questions.explain: Prompts are not permission controls; least privilege lives in config, credentials and server-side authorisation.

learnMore.en: A prompt only asks the model. If the credential allows deletion, the delete can still happen. Take the power away at the credential or server.
learnMore.hi: Prompt sirf model se kehta hai. Credential delete allow karta hai to delete ho sakta hai. Power credential ya server par hatao.

questions.q: An MCP server receives the client's access token and forwards it to a downstream API to save a login step. What is wrong with this?
options: Little, because forwarding the token keeps the user's identity intact
The token must be made longer-lived so that the downstream API can accept it at some later time
It is wrong when the token is stored in the model's context window
Token pass-through is forbidden, since a token is meant for the server that checked it
questions.explain: Tokens have an audience and must be validated by the server they were issued for; no token pass-through.

learnMore.en: A token is made for one destination. Sending it onward lets another service use it in the wrong place. Get a separate token.
learnMore.hi: Token ek destination ke liye bana hota hai. Aage bhejne par koi aur service use galat jagah laga sakti hai. Alag token lo.

questions.q: A mature command-line tool already does exactly what an agent needs. A teammate proposes a new MCP server around it. What is the best response?
options: Use the existing CLI, since wrapping a mature CLI in a new server duplicates what works
Build the MCP server, because every integration should go through MCP by default in every situation
Replace the CLI with a sub-agent that re-implements the same logic
Rewrite the CLI in the agent's own language so it can run in process
questions.explain: The protocol should follow the constraint; a mature CLI is already a valid answer.

learnMore.en: If a tool already works, do not rebuild it. A new wrapper only adds work and one more thing to maintain.
learnMore.hi: Jo tool pehle se kaam kar raha hai use dobara mat banao. Naya wrapper sirf kaam aur maintenance badhata hai.

questions.q: A support assistant has run for three months. After last Tuesday's knowledge-base re-index, error rate, P95 latency and cost per request are unchanged, yet escalations rise and satisfaction dips. What should the team add?
options: A tighter P95 latency alert, so the team is warned sooner about slower replies that users could see
An alert on a rise in HTTP 500 errors, so that failures are noticed straight away by the on-call
Sampled quality checks on production responses, plus retrieval-score tracking with drift alerts
Logging prompts and responses indefinitely, so engineers can review them later
questions.explain: Nothing loud moved; only the quality layer catches fluent failures, and retrieval drift points at the re-index.

learnMore.en: The server looks healthy, but the answers got worse. Only a check on answer quality can see this. Retrieval scores show the re-index problem.
learnMore.hi: Server theek dikh raha hai, par answers kharab ho gaye. Sirf answer quality check yeh pakad sakta hai. Retrieval scores re-index ki problem dikhate hain.

questions.q: An overnight research job makes company briefs in about 90 seconds each, including re-ranking and a figure-verification pass. An engineer proposes removing both to reach 25 seconds. What is the best response?
options: Approve it, because a cut of more than 70% in time is worth a small loss in answer quality on briefs
Remove verification but keep re-ranking, since one of them is enough
Switch to streaming, because it makes the overnight job complete faster
Keep both: latency is not binding overnight and verification guards the costliest failure
questions.explain: Nobody waits on an overnight job, so spending time on accuracy is the right trade; streaming does not help batch work.

learnMore.en: Speed only matters if someone waits. Overnight, nobody does. So keep the steps that protect accuracy.
learnMore.hi: Speed tab zaroori hai jab koi intezaar kare. Raat ke job mein koi nahi karta. Isliye accuracy bachane wale steps rakho.

questions.q: A restaurant voice-ordering agent has nine tools, almost all used on every call, and the prefix is already cached. Calls are live. A teammate proposes tool search to save tokens. What should you choose?
options: Defer all nine tools, because progressive discovery is cheaper
Keep monolithic loading: nothing to save, and discovery adds latency on a voice path
Adopt tool search but keep the three most-used tools non-deferred
Remove the least-used tools, since fewer tools means better accuracy for the agent on live calls
questions.explain: Breadth is not bloat: with a small, fully used, cached catalog, discovery only adds a round trip.

learnMore.en: Tool search saves tokens when the list is long and mostly unused. Here the list is short and all used, so search only adds delay.
learnMore.hi: Tool search tab kaam aata hai jab list lambi aur zyada unused ho. Yahan list chhoti aur sab use hoti hai, to search sirf delay badhata hai.

questions.q: A claims assistant on live phone calls has a P95 time-to-first-token of 9 seconds against a target of 4. The prompt carries a large repeated prefix, plus today's date and the adjuster's name at the top. What is the best first move?
options: Switch the whole system to the smallest model, since a smaller model is the fastest fix available
Drop retrieval depth to the minimum, because less context means faster responses
Move the date and name out of the system prompt so the prefix caches, and parallelise lookups
Add a verification pass to each claim to raise accuracy before the call
questions.explain: Static-first ordering with prompt caching is the usual latency answer; a blanket smaller model risks a fluent accuracy failure.

learnMore.en: Put the parts that never change first and the changing parts last. The cache can then reuse the start. Independent lookups can also run together.
learnMore.hi: Jo hissa kabhi nahi badalta use pehle rakho, badalne wala baad mein. Cache shuru reuse kar leta hai. Independent lookups saath chala sakte ho.

questions.q: A team says its SLA is time to first token, and the users are people chatting live. Which latency tactic helps?
options: Streaming, because it makes the wait feel shorter for a person reading the output
None, since streaming does not change what the user experiences
Waiting for the whole answer, because the user needs the complete text before they can start reading
Batch processing, because it returns the answers together at the end
questions.explain: For a chat user the SLA is time to first token and streaming helps; for a downstream system that needs the full payload it does not.

learnMore.en: A person starts reading when the first words appear. Streaming brings those words sooner. A machine that needs the whole result gets no benefit.
learnMore.hi: Insaan pehle shabd dikhte hi padhna shuru karta hai. Streaming wo shabd jaldi laata hai. Jis machine ko poora result chahiye use fayda nahi.

questions.q: A team's extraction system scores 97% on 200 handpicked documents, but production is mostly messy scans, multilingual emails and out-of-scope messages. Which fix is best?
options: Rebuild the set by stratified random sampling of production traffic plus seeded edge cases
Add 2,000 more examples chosen the same way, so the set is bigger and steadier
Switch the headline metric to F1, because it handles imbalance better than plain accuracy ever can
Replace the rule-based grading with a model judge to score messy documents better
questions.explain: The defect is coverage, not arithmetic or grader choice; a bigger handpicked set is only a more confident wrong number.

learnMore.en: The test set does not look like real traffic. Fix that first. A new metric or grader on the same weak data changes nothing.
learnMore.hi: Test set asli traffic jaisa nahi hai. Pehle yeh theek karo. Wahi weak data par naya metric ya grader kuch nahi badalta.

questions.q: A prompt tweak lifts the golden-set score from 60% to 70% on a 10-document set. Should you ship it?
options: Yes, because a 10-point gain is large enough to be treated as real on any set of documents
Yes, once you also switch the metric to F1 so that you can confirm the gain is a real one
Not yet: re-run the unchanged system to measure the noise floor first
Not yet: add ten more documents chosen by the same team in the same way
questions.explain: With only 10 documents, one item moves the score 10 points and non-determinism can flip documents alone.

learnMore.en: On a tiny set, one document changes the score by 10 points, and the model may answer differently each run. Measure that noise before you trust a gain.
learnMore.hi: Chhote set mein ek document score 10 points badal deta hai, aur model har baar alag answer de sakta hai. Gain par bharosa karne se pehle noise naapo.

questions.q: A document extraction system reports 97% accuracy overall, yet customers complain about handwritten receipts. Why is the headline number misleading?
options: Handwritten receipts should be left out of the evaluation, since they are rare in the traffic
The overall number hides a slice where failures cluster, so measure per stratum
97% is too high to be believed, so the whole evaluation must be repeated
Accuracy is the wrong family; latency and cost are what traces can show
questions.explain: An aggregate score can hide a failing slice; stratified sampling keeps each population visible.

learnMore.en: Most documents are easy and push the average up. A small hard group can still fail a lot. Look at each group separately.
learnMore.hi: Zyada documents aasaan hain aur average upar le jaate hain. Chhota mushkil group phir bhi bahut fail ho sakta hai. Har group alag dekho.

questions.q: A team uses a model as judge to grade outputs on a 1-to-10 scale, and has never checked it against human labels. What is the best improvement?
options: Keep the 1-to-10 scale but ask the judge to explain its score in more detail each time it grades
Trust the judge, because a model grading another model is unreliable otherwise in practice
Replace the judge with a rule-based grader for each kind of quality check
Explicit rubric criteria and binary verdicts with a reason, calibrated against human labels
questions.explain: A model grader is trustworthy only after measured agreement with humans; a bad judge turns errors into scores.

learnMore.en: A judge is only useful if its verdicts match what humans would say. Check this on labelled examples first. Yes or no with a reason is easier to check than 1 to 10.
learnMore.hi: Judge tabhi kaam ka hai jab uska verdict insaan ke verdict se mile. Pehle labelled examples par check karo. Yes ya no aur reason, 1 se 10 se aasaan hai.

questions.q: A golden-set row is a customer message asking about a shipment, with no invoice in it, and the expected fields are null. What is this row for?
options: It is an edge case meant to test how well the model reads handwriting
It is a noise-floor row, used to measure how much the scores change between one run and the next
A guard row: if the model invents a vendor or invoice number, the check fails
It is a stratum row, used to give small document types more weight
questions.explain: Guard rows have a null or refusal as the correct answer, so fabricated output fails.

learnMore.en: The right answer here is "nothing found". If the model fills in an invoice anyway, it made it up, and the test catches it.
learnMore.hi: Yahan sahi answer "kuch nahi mila" hai. Model phir bhi invoice bhar de to usne bana liya, aur test use pakad leta hai.

questions.q: A support lead wants to roll out a "sharper" new system prompt to 100% of 2,000 daily tickets without an evaluation. Which approach is right?
options: Run both prompts on the same frozen golden set, with metric and threshold fixed first
Ship on volume, since five days of tickets is a large enough sample to be sure of the result
Ask the model which prompt it prefers and ship the winner that it picks out by itself
Run a one-day 5% canary and ship the new prompt everywhere if it looks better on that day
questions.explain: Ship on volume is not evidence for a vibe; the model is not a valid self-grader; the canary has no pre-declared threshold.

learnMore.en: A fair test uses the same data for both prompts and a pass mark set before the results. Then you can believe the result.
learnMore.hi: Fair test mein dono prompts ko same data milta hai aur pass mark pehle se tay hota hai. Tab result par bharosa ho sakta hai.

questions.q: A restaurant launches a new menu in festival week and sales rise 40%. Did the menu cause it?
options: Yes, because sales rose right after the launch, so the menu was clearly the cause of it
Yes, if the rise lasts longer than one full week and the sales stay high afterwards
No, because a menu change does not affect sales in a measurable way
Nobody can say: the festival is a confounder; compare both menus in one week
questions.explain: Both variants must be compared in the same time window so that outside events hit both equally.

learnMore.en: The festival may have pushed sales up anyway. To judge the menu, test both menus in the same week.
learnMore.hi: Tyohaar ki wajah se bhi sales badh sakti hain. Menu judge karne ke liye dono menus ek hi hafte mein test karo.

questions.q: A coding assistant's suggestion acceptance fell from 34% to 27% in a week, with latency, errors and cost flat. Three things changed: a provider model update, a shorter system prompt, and larger repo-indexing chunks. How do you find the cause?
options: Roll back the model first, since a provider update is the most likely cause of a drop like this one
Flip one change at a time on a frozen golden set and find the one that flips the failure
Rewrite the system prompt again, since it was the change that landed nearest to the drop in acceptance
Add more chunks to retrieval, since the larger chunks may have lost some of the content in each file
questions.explain: In the case study the new model and new prompt kept the baseline; only the larger chunks broke it, by splitting function signatures.

learnMore.en: When several things changed, test them one by one on the same data. The one that brings back the failure is the cause. The loudest change is not always guilty.
learnMore.hi: Jab kai cheezein badli hon, ek-ek karke same data par test karo. Jo failure wapas laaye wahi karan hai. Sabse loud change doshi nahi hota.

questions.q: A pipeline gets 91% field accuracy overall, but dense multi-table statements, about 10% of volume, sit at 58%. The prompt was tightened twice and retrieval is verified. The cost ceiling is firm. What next?
options: Rewrite the prompt a third time with even more explicit criteria
Route the hard class to a larger tier or split it into per-table passes
Upgrade the whole pipeline to the largest model for every document
Recalibrate the eval set so that the hard class counts for much less in the overall score reported
questions.explain: Prompt and retrieval are already cleared, so the model tier is the remaining suspect, and only for the hard 10%.

learnMore.en: The easy 90% is fine, so leave it alone. Give only the hard 10% more power. This fixes the weak part within the budget.
learnMore.hi: Aasaan 90% theek hai, use mat chhedo. Sirf mushkil 10% ko zyada power do. Isse budget mein weak part theek hota hai.

questions.q: After a weekend move to a new document store, a legal assistant cites superseded policy versions. Latency, errors and cost are unchanged, and the old documents are still in the new store. What should you check first?
options: The system prompt, by adding a rule that tells the model to prefer the newest policy version
A validation pass that rejects any answer which mentions an old version of the policy document
A larger model, so it can work out which version is current
Retrieval and its metadata, since the new store may not serve versions correctly
questions.explain: After a data change, the retrieval layer is the first suspect; the model comes last.

learnMore.en: The data moved, so the first thing to check is how it is found and which version comes back. Prompts and models come later.
learnMore.hi: Data move hua, to pehle dekho wo kaise milta hai aur kaunsa version aata hai. Prompt aur model baad mein dekho.

questions.q: A customer support assistant runs live chat with a 4-second P95 SLA, and finance wants a cut this quarter. Which change is the right one?
options: Move the nightly summary of closed tickets to the Message Batches API
Send the complex claims questions to the smallest tier too, to cut the model price paid
Cut retrieval from 12 chunks to 3 and skip re-running the evals
Buy the one-hour cache TTL for the conversation prefix
questions.explain: A nightly job is batch-shaped and nobody waits; the others risk quiet accuracy loss or pay for a TTL chat does not need.

learnMore.en: Batch is cheaper when nobody waits. The nightly job fits. Changes to live chat risk quality or cost more.
learnMore.hi: Batch tab sasta hai jab koi intezaar nahi karta. Raat ka job fit hai. Live chat mein badlav quality girate hain ya cost badhate hain.

questions.q: Automated code reviews block PR merges. A developer wants to move them to the Message Batches API to cut cost. What is the main concern?
options: Batch reviews are of lower quality than standard ones because they run at a discount to the user
Batch does not accept code files, because it takes plain-text chat messages as its input
Batch gives no delivery guarantee in a useful time, so the pipeline could time out
Batch reviews are more expensive than standard reviews
questions.explain: Anything that blocks a human or a pipeline step cannot use batch, which has a 24-hour window and no latency promise.

learnMore.en: Batch can take up to a day. If a merge is waiting, that delay blocks the team. Use batch only when nobody waits.
learnMore.hi: Batch mein ek din tak lag sakta hai. Merge ruka ho to team ruk jaati hai. Batch tabhi use karo jab koi intezaar na kare.

questions.q: Over two weeks, cost per request is up 40% while accuracy is flat and no deploys happened. Cache reads fell from about 70% of input to near zero after a brand refresh added a greeting line to the system prompt. What is the fix?
options: Upgrade to a larger model tier, so each answer needs fewer tokens
Increase retrieval depth, so the model gets more context per request
Move the whole service to the Message Batches API so that every call gets the batch discount instead
Restore the previous system prompt and move changeable text out of the cached prefix
questions.explain: A larger tier would spend more against a problem the eval set does not show; the cache broke because the prefix changed.

learnMore.en: The greeting changed the start of the prompt, so the cache stopped matching. Put the changing text last and the cache works again.
learnMore.hi: Greeting ne prompt ka shuru badal diya, to cache match nahi hua. Badalne wala text aakhir mein rakho, cache phir chalega.

questions.q: An insurer's claims traffic rises every monsoon, and raw monthly spend rises with it. Should a raw-spend alert page the on-call engineer?
options: Yes, because spend above last month's total should be treated as a possible incident by on-call
No: volume growth is the business succeeding; alert on cost per request instead
Yes, on weekends, when the on-call load is lower
No, because costs should not be monitored with alerts, and are reviewed in the monthly meeting
questions.explain: Alert on ratios and unit economics, not on raw counts.

learnMore.en: More claims mean more spend, and that is normal. Cost per request only rises if something went wrong. So alert on that.
learnMore.hi: Zyada claims matlab zyada kharcha, aur yeh normal hai. Cost per request tabhi badhta hai jab kuch galat ho. Isliye usi par alert karo.

questions.q: Which factor of the spend equation does the Message Batches API change?
options: The price per token, because batch picks the smallest model tier
The tokens per request, because batch compresses the prompt automatically
The shape of the requests, because it processes work later at a discount
The cache hit ratio, because batch pre-warms the cache before running
